practical.title: File I/O and Command-Line Arguments — Intensive Practical Lab
practical.summary: An intensive, multi-scene lab that guides learners through observing, modifying, extending, and verifying a C file-copy utility that uses command-line arguments and character-by-character file I/O.
practical.sourceActivity: File I/O and Command-Line Arguments — Intensive Practical Lab

coachingPrompts: What do you predict will happen before you run it?
What evidence shows that your change worked?
Can you explain the result in your own words?

files.content:
Hello Cohortia!
This is a test file.

tasks.title: Scene 1 — Observe & Understand (2–4 min)
tasks.narratorGuide: Hello! In this first scene you'll run the provided file-copy utility without changing any code. Notice how the program validates argc, opens files with fopen(), loops using fgetc() until EOF, writes each character with fputc(), and finally closes both streams. Watching the program run gives context for later edits — you'll see the success message and then inspect the copied file to confirm byte-by-byte fidelity.

tasks.title: Scene 2 — Modify & Experiment (4–6 min)
tasks.narratorGuide: Now you'll modify the running program to count how many characters it copies. This is a focused change: add an integer counter initialized to zero, increment it inside the copy loop, and print the byte count before the success message. This reinforces thinking about loop invariants and gives observable feedback you can verify against the source file size.

tasks.title: Scene 3 — Build & Integrate (4–8 min)
tasks.narratorGuide: In this scene you'll integrate two practical improvements. First, add a defensive check that refuses to copy when the input and output filenames are identical — this prevents data loss. Second, open files with "rb" and "wb" modes so the same program works with binary files. Both changes are small but meaningful in real-world tools: filename validation avoids surprising behavior, and binary modes preserve raw bytes.

tasks.title: Scene 4 — Verify & Extend (3–5 min)
tasks.narratorGuide: Now confirm the program fails gracefully when misused: run it with no arguments to see the usage message, run it with a nonexistent input file to see the file-open error, and consider how you'd add a -v flag to print progress each N bytes. These verifications are critical — they show your program anticipates bad input rather than crashing silently.
